outcome: As of 10 Oct 2026 the problem is still open in every source I could read: no accepted proof exists, and the only claimed complete proof (Tanvith Reddy, figshare preprint, 30 Apr to 1 May 2025) is unrefereed and I could not verify it. Post-26-Jan-2024 events are a heuristic approximation (Lambard, arXiv, Nov 2024, self-described as not a proof), an unrefereed 'structural framework' with an argued obstruction (Shang Yu Chen, Cambridge Open Engage, 3 Aug 2026, no proof claim on the page), a variant with the sum taken over an arithmetic progression (Dong, Nguyen and Zaharescu, arXiv, 4 Aug 2026, different question), and a sum-free-set paper sharing the name (Beker, arXiv, Jan 2025, different problem).
problem_asks: Statement: 'Is 1^1 + 2^1 = 3^1 the only solution to the Erdős–Moser equation?' The equation is 1^k + 2^k + ... + (m-1)^k = m^k in positive integers m and k. Parts: (i) k = 1: the sum 1 + 2 + ... + (m-1) = m forces m = 3, so 1^1 + 2^1 = 3^1 is the only solution with k = 1; this part is elementary and is the trivial solution the statement names. (ii) k >= 2: show there is no pair (m, k) of positive integers with k >= 2 satisfying the equation. The question as worded asks for the 'only solution' claim, i.e. (i) and (ii) together. It does not ask for finiteness of the solution set or for size bounds on m, which are background.

events.what_happened: Leo Moser, 'On the diophantine equation 1^n + 2^n + ... + (m-1)^n = m^n', Scripta Mathematica 19 (1953) 84-88, as cited by the Wikipedia article (the primary paper was not opened). Per Pieter Moree's arXiv abstract (1011.2940), Moser showed that if the equation has an integer solution with k >= 2 then m > 10^(10^6); per the Wikipedia article as fetched, Moser also showed k must be even and m-1 squarefree. Search-result summaries also report that Moser settled odd exponents; I did not verify that from a primary source.
events.delivers: Restricted results: (a) no solution with odd k (per secondary reports only); (b) any solution with k >= 2 has k even and m > 10^(10^6); (c) m-1 squarefree (per Wikipedia). Does not settle even k.
events.remains: Existence of solutions with even k >= 2 and m beyond the 10^(10^6) bound; whether the solution set is finite; the full nonexistence claim.

checked_by.qualification: Number theorist who has worked on this equation for over a decade (arXiv 1011.2940 and related papers)
checked_by.what_they_did: Gave a simplified re-derivation of Moser's argument via a von Staudt-Clausen type theorem; the abstract says 'With the hindsight of more than 50 years his proof can be somewhat simplified'

events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture: restricted cases excluded and any solution must be astronomically large.

events.what_happened: Schinzel (1987) showed that in any solution m is odd. Known to me only from search-result summaries of arXiv 1010.2275 and arXiv 2306.05168; neither the 1987 paper nor those arXiv texts were opened, so the journal and exact wording are unverified.
events.delivers: Restriction: any solution has m odd (per summaries). Does not establish existence or nonexistence.
events.remains: Solutions with m odd (all k >= 2); the rest of the problem.
events.doubts: Recorded from secondary summaries only; not checked against the 1987 paper.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Bronislaw Krzysztofek, Zeszyty Naukowe WSP w Katowicach 5 (1966) 47-54 (Polish), as reported by the Wikipedia article (primary not opened). Reported bounds: m/(k+1) < 3/2 and m-1 cannot be prime. The Wikipedia text as fetched is partly garbled, so the exact form of the inequality chain is unverified.
events.delivers: Restrictions on any solution (as reported): m-1 is not prime; m/(k+1) < 3/2.
events.remains: Existence of any solution; the rest of the problem.

checked_by.who: Zeszyty Naukowe Wyzszej Szkoly Pedagogicznej w Katowicach (university journal)
checked_by.qualification: University journal publishing the paper; refereeing practice not verified

events.doubts: Known only from the Wikipedia article's summary; primary not opened.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Moree, te Riele and Urbanowicz, Mathematics of Computation 63 (1994) 799-815, as cited by the Wikipedia article (primary not opened). Reported results: lcm(1,...,200) divides k; m is congruent to 3 mod 2^(ord_2(k)+3); any prime factor of m is irregular and greater than 10000.
events.delivers: Divisibility and congruence restrictions on any solution (as reported); no bound on m stated in the summary.
events.remains: Existence of any solution; the rest of the problem.
events.doubts: Known only from the Wikipedia summary; the ord_2 and irregular-prime statements are as reported and unverified.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Butske, Jaje and Mayernik, Mathematics of Computation 69 (1999) 407-420, as cited by the Wikipedia article and search summaries (primary not opened). Refined Moser's method by computing quantities in his proof rather than estimating them, reporting m > 1.485 x 10^9,321,155 for any solution with k >= 2.
events.delivers: Lower bound on m for any solution with k >= 2: m > 1.485 x 10^9,321,155 (as reported). Moves the bound on m; does not settle existence.
events.remains: Existence of solutions with m above this bound; the rest of the problem.
events.doubts: Superseded by Gallot, Moree and Zudilin (2009); the stated figure is from secondary reports and unverified against the paper.
events.direction: Bound moved in the direction of the conjecture; not a settlement.

events.what_happened: Bernd Christian Kellner, Gottingen diploma thesis 'Uber irregulare Paare hoherer Ordnungen' (2002), as cited by the Wikipedia article (thesis not opened). Reported result: k is a multiple of 2^3 . 3# . 5# . 7# . 19# . 1000# (# = primorial) and k exceeds 5.7462 x 10^427.
events.delivers: Divisibility restriction on k for any solution, and a size bound on k (as reported). Does not settle existence.
events.remains: Existence of any solution; the rest of the problem.
events.doubts: Unrefereed diploma thesis; no independent check found. Known only from Wikipedia's summary; which quantity the size bound applies to is not stated in what I read.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Yves Gallot, Pieter Moree and Wadim Zudilin, 'The Erdos-Moser equation 1^k + 2^k + ... + (m-1)^k = m^k revisited using continued fractions', arXiv:0907.1356, first posted 8 July 2009 (only version), published Mathematics of Computation 80 (2011) 1221-1237. The main theorem (Theorem 3, read in the ar5iv text) states that for any integer pair (m, k) with k >= 2 satisfying the equation, m > 2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416. The abstract states the round figure m > 10^(10^9), reached 'in no more than 10 hours with 3 x 10^9 digits of log 2', and says Moser's approach 'cannot be improved to reach' m > 10^(10^7). The method shows 2k/(2m-3) is a convergent of log 2.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (8 Jul 2009, per arXiv abstract page). Journal version Math. Comp. 80 (2011), 1221-1237.
events.delivers: Lower bound for any solution with k >= 2: m > 2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416 (Theorem 3 as read). This moves the bound on m, the quantity the problem's equation fixes; it excludes only m below that threshold and says nothing about larger m.
events.remains: Whether a solution exists with m above 2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416; the nonexistence claim for all k >= 2; finiteness.

checked_by.who: Mathematics of Computation editors and referees (American Mathematical Society)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, Math. Comp. 80 (2011) 1221-1237

events.directly_checkable: The continued-fraction computation on the digits of log 2 can in principle be re-run; I did not re-run it.
events.doubts: The abstract's round figure (10^(10^9)) and Theorem 3's figure (2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416) differ in form; I record the theorem as the stronger statement, and both appear in the record. The result depends on about 3 x 10^9 digits of log 2 computed correctly; I found no independent recomputation.
events.direction: Bound moved in the direction of the conjecture; not a settlement.

ai.disclosed_cost: 'in no more than 10 hours with 3 x 10^9 digits of log 2' (arXiv:0907.1356 text, via ar5iv)

events.what_happened: Jonathan Sondow and Emmanuel Tsukerman, 'The p-adic order of power sums, the Erdos-Moser equation, and Bernoulli numbers', arXiv:1401.0322 (v1 1 Jan 2014). Abstract: the equation 'remains unresolved to this day'; the authors derive necessary divisibility properties of power sums and a restrictive Egyptian fraction equation that any solution must satisfy, and motivate Moser's approach.
events.delivers: Necessary conditions on any solution (divisibility of power sums; an Egyptian fraction equation). Not a bound on m and not a nonexistence result.
events.remains: Whether any solution exists; the rest of the problem.
events.direction: Necessary conditions; does not indicate whether solutions exist.

events.what_happened: Kieren MacMillan and Jonathan Sondow, 'Divisibility of power sums and the generalized Erdos-Moser equation', arXiv:1010.2275 (October 2010). Known to me only from search-result summaries; not opened. Reported content: the highest power of 2 dividing a power sum, and an elementary proof that for the generalized equation 1^n + ... + (m-1)^n = a m^n any solution has m odd (Moree's result), which covers a = 1.
events.delivers: Restriction: m odd in any solution, including the a = 1 case (per summary). Does not establish nonexistence.
events.remains: Existence of solutions with m odd; the rest of the problem.
events.doubts: From search-result summaries only; not opened.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Pieter Moree, 'Moser's mathemagical work on the equation 1^k + 2^k + ... + (m-1)^k = m^k', arXiv:1011.2940, submitted 12 Nov 2010, revised 26 Mar 2011. Abstract (as read): gives a further, simplified proof of Moser's result (m > 10^(10^6) for k >= 2) via a von Staudt-Clausen type theorem; derives a new result from divisibility properties of the numbers 2^(2e+1)+1; shows that certain Erdos-Moser type equations from a recent paper of Kellner can be solved completely.
events.delivers: A re-proof of Moser's 1953 bound; a new divisibility restriction from 2^(2e+1)+1 (as reported); complete solution of certain neighbouring Kellner-type equations (which equations is not stated in the abstract I read). Nothing here bears on the a = 1 equation beyond the re-proof.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.direction: Restricted results and re-proofs; no conclusion for the problem as stated.

events.what_happened: Ioulia N. Baoulina and Pieter Moree, 'Forbidden integer ratios of consecutive power sums', arXiv:1510.06064 (20 Oct 2015). Abstract: studies Kellner's conjecture that S_k(m+1)/S_k(m) is never an integer for m >= 4 where S_k(m) = 1^k + ... + (m-1)^k. To exclude a ratio rho one must show (rho-1) S_k(m) = m^k has no non-trivial solutions. The paper excludes integer ratios 3 <= rho <= 1501 and, assuming a conjecture on irregular primes, a density-1 set of ratios.
events.delivers: Nonexistence of non-trivial solutions of (rho-1) S_k(m) = m^k for rho in 3..1501 (coefficient a = rho-1 in 2..1500), and for a density-1 set under an irregular-primes conjecture. Neighbouring equation with a != 1. The Erdos-Moser equation itself corresponds to rho = 2 (a = 1), which lies outside the excluded range.
events.remains: The a = 1 case (the Erdos-Moser equation itself) and the other coefficients outside the stated ranges.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (generalized coefficient); does not settle a = 1 and the abstract does not claim to.

events.what_happened: Ioulia N. Baoulina, 'On the unsolvability of certain equations of Erdos-Moser type', arXiv:1804.04646 (v1 12 Apr 2018; v2 26 Jun 2018), published Elemente der Mathematik 74 (2019) 1-9. Abstract (as read): for many integers a, a T_k(m) = (2m+1)^k has no solutions in positive integers k, m, where T_k(m) = sum over j=1..m of (2j-1)^k; the paper conjectures that T_k(m+1)/T_k(m) is never an integer. The abstract presents a-coefficient unsolvability for the odd-number sums; it does not claim that a S_k(m) = m^k is resolved for a = 1.
events.revisions: v1 12 Apr 2018; v2 26 Jun 2018; journal Elem. Math. 74 (2019) 1-9.
events.delivers: Unsolvability of a T_k(m) = (2m+1)^k for many a. This is a different power-sum equation (odd-number sums); it does not establish the Erdos-Moser equation for any a.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (different power-sum equation); not a settlement of the problem.

events.what_happened: Jonathan Sondow and Kieren MacMillan, 'Primary pseudoperfect numbers, arithmetic progressions, and the Erdos-Moser equation', The American Mathematical Monthly 124(3) (2017) 232-240. A later arXiv posting (arXiv:1812.06566, 17 Dec 2018) carries the same paper. The arXiv abstract says the result is conditional on the authors' conjecture about primary pseudoperfect numbers, and gives: any non-trivial solution of 1^n + ... + k^n = (k+1)^n has k > 10^(3.99 x 10^20). In this problem's notation the bound applies to m-1. The exact hypothesis is not in the abstract; a search summary says Proposition 6 assumes there are no primary pseudoperfect numbers with r >= 33 prime factors, which I did not verify.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 17 Dec 2018, a later posting of the 2017 journal paper. A search summary of the Zenodo record gives 'Published January 1, 2017'; I did not reconcile this with the issue date (vol. 124 no. 3 is March 2017).
events.delivers: Conditional lower bound: under the authors' hypothesis on primary pseudoperfect numbers, m > 10^(3.99 x 10^20). Not unconditional; moves the bound only if the hypothesis holds.
events.remains: Unconditional nonexistence for k >= 2; the hypothesis on primary pseudoperfect numbers.

checked_by.who: American Mathematical Monthly editors and referees (Mathematical Association of America)

events.doubts: The result is conditional on a conjecture about primary pseudoperfect numbers. A search summary (OEIS A054377, not opened) reports a new term added 13 Apr 2026 by Martins and Wang, which could bear on that conjecture. A 2026 preprint on the same objects (arXiv 2605.21518, opened) says nothing about Sondow and MacMillan's conjecture or this bound. I did not verify whether any new term affects the hypothesis the bound actually uses.
events.direction: Conditional bound in the direction of the conjecture; not a settlement.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the general Erdos-Moser equation via the notion of olloids', AfricArXiv preprint (repository record 1/1362, DOI 10.14293/111.000/000043.v1). The repository abstract reads: 'We introduce and develop the notion of the olloid. We apply this notion to study a variant and a generalized version of the Erdos-Moser equation under some special local condition.' The repository page I read shows no posting date; the August 2022 date comes from a search summary. No theorem about the original equation is visible.
events.delivers: Not determinable from the abstract: it applies the olloid notion to a variant and a generalized version under an unspecified local condition. It does not state a result about the original equation.
events.remains: All of the problem as stated.
events.doubts: Repository states the work is not peer-reviewed. The full PDF was not reachable (one mirror failed DNS resolution; the repository download link was not fetched). No response to the work found in search.
events.direction: Unclear from the abstract; does not claim to settle the problem.

events.what_happened: Guillaume Lambard, 'An Analytical Exploration of the Erdos-Moser Equation sum_{i=1}^{m-1} i^k = m^k Using Approximation Methods', arXiv:2411.13146, first submitted 20 Nov 2024, v2 21 Nov 2024, v3 11 Apr 2025. Replaces the discrete sum with a continuous function via the Euler-MacLaurin formula, then looks for integer roots of the resulting polynomial with the rational root theorem. Concludes the approximation supports the known solution (k, m) = (1, 3) and suggests no other positive integer solutions for k >= 2. The abstract says 'it does not constitute a definitive proof'. The text read (first 100,000 of about 130,768 characters) contains no acknowledgements and no mention of software, AI or LLM use.
events.revisions: v1 20 Nov 2024; v2 21 Nov 2024; v3 11 Apr 2025 (arXiv abstract page). No journal reference found.
events.delivers: A heuristic approximation, self-described as not a proof: it suggests no solutions for k >= 2 and is consistent with the k = 1 solution m = 3. Establishes no rigorous nonexistence.
events.remains: The whole problem: the rigorous nonexistence for k >= 2 and, in the author's words, 'fully rigorous approaches' are still needed.
events.time_since_posted: about 23 months since v1 (20 Nov 2024 to 10 Oct 2026); about 18 months since v3
events.doubts: The author's own caveats: omitting correction terms in the Euler-MacLaurin expansion 'could mask genuine solutions' and 'prevents a fully rigorous Diophantine closure'. The method is approximate by design, and the paper makes no proof claim.
events.direction: Heuristic evidence in the direction of the conjecture (no further solutions); not a proof.

events.what_happened: Adrian Beker, 'The Erdos-Moser sum-free set problem via improved bounds for k-configurations', arXiv:2501.10203, submitted 17 Jan 2025 (the arXiv page lists a later revision dated 2 Oct 2026). Concerns the Erdos-Moser sum-free set problem: a subset of integers with no sum of two distinct elements in the set. Gives a set of size (log|A|)^(1+Omega(1)) with that property, improving a bound due to Shao, and so a new proof of a lower bound for that problem.
events.revisions: v1 17 Jan 2025; a later revision dated 2 Oct 2026 per the arXiv page (content not read).
events.delivers: Discounted: a bound on sum-free subsets (a different problem that shares the Erdos-Moser name). Says nothing about the power-sum equation.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different question sharing a name.

events.what_happened: Tanvith Reddy, 'A Self-Contained Proof of the Erdos-Moser Equation's Uniqueness', figshare preprint (not on arXiv), DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.28899983. Figshare metadata: first online 30 Apr 2025, four versions, published 1 May 2025 (version 4, 04:22 UTC); CC BY 4.0. Description as read through the figshare API: the equation has no positive-integer solutions except (m, k) = (3, 1); the method introduces a strictly decreasing real-valued function f(k) to analyse the uniqueness of real roots for fixed m; non-integrality of solutions for 4 <= m <= 100 is verified numerically; for m > 100 the argument relies on 'existing analytical results from the literature' (the results are not named in what I read). The author calls it a 'direct, fully elementary proof'. The PDF was not readable through my tools (see incomplete).
events.revisions: Versions 1-4 posted 30 Apr to 1 May 2025 (figshare). Content of the earlier versions not read.
events.delivers: Claimed complete resolution: no solutions with k >= 2, and k = 1 gives only m = 3. As claimed, m <= 100 is handled by computation and m > 100 by cited existing analytic results; I could not identify those results from what I read.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds. The claim is unverified.
events.directly_checkable: The finite check for 4 <= m <= 100 is in principle reproducible by anyone; I did not run it. The monotonicity argument that carries the rest is in the PDF, which I could not read.
events.doubts: (1) Not refereed; figshare preprint; no review, critique, comment or endorsement found in search or on the figshare pages read. (2) The scope for m > 100 rests on existing analytic results that the abstract does not name. The results I read about this equation are lower bounds on m (Moser 1953; Gallot, Moree and Zudilin 2009: no solution below about 2.7 x 10^(1.67 x 10^9)). Such bounds exclude small m but not all large m. I could not see how existing results rule out every m > 100. This is my inference from the cited bounds, not a checked error; the cited results in the PDF would settle it. (3) The title and 'fully elementary' label sit beside a numerical check and external citations, which the author's own abstract states. (4) The encyclopedia silence: the Wikipedia article as fetched (last edited 26 Dec 2025 per the page) describes no result after 2009-2010 and does not mention this preprint.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture: no solutions with k >= 2, so (3, 1) is the only solution.

events.what_happened: Shang Yu Chen, 'Parity Decomposition and Logarithmic Obstructions in the Erdos-Moser Equation', Cambridge Open Engage working paper, DOI 10.33774/coe-2026-98l21, posted 3 Aug 2026 as version 1, CC BY 4.0, marked as not peer-reviewed. The abstract as read on the page: 'This work develops a structural analytic framework for the Erdos-Moser equation'; using parity decomposition and logarithmic projection it 'identif[ies] a stable first-order defect of size C_k/(m ln m) for all k >= 2', attributed to the 'nonlinear collapse of the parity progression'; it argues this produces 'a logarithmic residue incompatible with the integer lattice', 'yielding a unified obstruction to non-linear solutions'. The author does not use the word 'proof' on the page. The full text is not viewable there. The comment section is empty.
events.revisions: Version 1 only, as listed on the page.
events.delivers: As stated in the abstract: an asymptotic defect for k >= 2 and an argued 'obstruction' to non-linear solutions. The abstract does not say that this rules out all solutions with k >= 2, and I could not determine the scope from it.
events.remains: Per the abstract's own language it is unclear. If the obstruction is valid as stated, it would cover k >= 2 for all m; the derivation is not visible to me.
events.directly_checkable: The defect is an asymptotic claim; a direct check would be its numerical size for small m and k, which the page does not supply.
events.doubts: (1) Only the abstract is visible; no derivation. (2) A 'first-order defect' of size C_k/(m ln m) is an asymptotic statement; how it excludes exact integer solutions needs an error term that the abstract does not mention. (3) Single author; no affiliation listed on the page; I did not check the author's publication record. (4) Not peer-reviewed, as the page states.
events.direction: Argued obstruction to non-linear solutions: points toward the conjecture (no solutions with k >= 2) if the obstruction holds. The author presents it as a framework, not a proof.

events.what_happened: Anji Dong, Vi Anh Nguyen and Alexandru Zaharescu, 'Erdos-Moser Equation in Arithmetic Progressions', arXiv:2608.03375, submitted 4 Aug 2026 (v1 only). Abstract (as read): the equation 1^k + ... + (m-1)^k = m^k is considered with the sum taken over an arithmetic progression; for k = 2 the paper proves that any solution's progression sum must consist of two or four terms, and in both cases there are infinitely many solutions, completely characterized. The abstract does not mention the Erdos-Moser conjecture.
events.delivers: Discounted: a variant in which the sum runs over an arithmetic progression, with results stated for k = 2. It does not address the sum over 1, ..., m-1 and does not change the answer to the problem as stated.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated (the unrestricted sum with k >= 2).
events.direction: Not applicable to the bullet's equation: a different question (sum over an arithmetic progression).

summary: The problem is open in every source I could read as of 10 Oct 2026, and no source credits an AI system with any part of it. I ran 40 web searches (the problem's name and variants, result-type words, recent work, AI terms, lab and benchmark announcements, and Lean and erdosproblems checks) and opened about 20 pages. The record holds 19 events. Before 2024: the classical restrictions and bounds (Moser 1953; Schinzel 1987; Krzysztofek 1966; Moree, te Riele and Urbanowicz 1994; Butske, Jaje and Mayernik 1999; Kellner 2002; Gallot, Moree and Zudilin 2009, whose theorem gives m > 2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416 for any solution with k >= 2), the conditional bound of Sondow and MacMillan (2017), and neighbouring generalisations (Baoulina and Moree 2015, Baoulina 2018, and an olloid preprint by Agama in 2022). Since 26 Jan 2024: Lambard (Nov 2024), a heuristic that says it is not a proof; Beker (Jan 2025), a different problem that shares the name; Reddy (30 Apr 2025), a claimed complete elementary proof on figshare; Chen (3 Aug 2026), an unrefereed 'framework' with an argued obstruction and no proof claim on the page; and Dong, Nguyen and Zaharescu (4 Aug 2026), a variant over arithmetic progressions for k = 2. Close calls: (a) Reddy. Whether this counts depends on its PDF, which I could not read. Its abstract, as summarised through the figshare API, says that m > 100 is handled by existing analytic results. The lower bounds on m that I could find exclude only small m, so I could not see how they would exclude all m > 100. That inference is mine, and the cited results would settle it. (b) Chen. The abstract's language is 'framework', 'identify' and 'yielding a unified obstruction'. It does not say 'prove', and I could not tell whether the argument is intended to cover all m for k >= 2. (c) Gallot et al. The abstract's round figure (10^(10^9)) and the theorem's figure (2.7139 x 10^1,667,658,416) disagree in form; I record the theorem as the stronger statement and the abstract figure as well. (d) The Wikipedia article as fetched has garbled exponents (for example 'm > 10^109' for Erdos's bound), so I used primary sources for the numbers. The AI search turned up nothing for this problem. The OpenAI Astra and unit-distance results, the DeepMind 700-conjecture study, AlphaProof Nexus, Aletheia, and the Erdos 728 and 767 work concern other problems. The Quanta articles of 3 Aug 2026 that I opened do not mention this equation. The FrontierMath Erdos benchmark's 68 problems (arXiv 2609.25050) do not include it on the reading I got of its appendix.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a different reading is that the Reddy preprint is a valid proof. It would then settle the problem as of 30 Apr 2025, and it involves no AI. The case rests on the author's claim that m > 100 is covered by analytic results he cites, and on a monotonicity lemma for a decreasing function f(k). If those cited results exist and cover all large m, my objection in the doubts field fails. The other reading is that Chen's 'obstruction' is a rigorous nonexistence argument for k >= 2, which would settle the problem as of 3 Aug 2026 if correct. The abstract does not establish either. The reading that the problem is still open rests on the absence of any refereed acceptance of either claim and on the author's own caveats for Lambard.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full Reddy PDF: the monotonicity lemma, the exact external results used for m > 100, and whether they cover all large m. (2) The full Chen text: whether the 'obstruction' is derived rigorously for all m, and whether it covers k >= 2 without leaving an error term. (3) Any refereed acceptance or expert write-up of either claim, or a Lean formalisation with no sorry. (4) The text of Sondow and MacMillan's Proposition 6 hypothesis and any new primary pseudoperfect number that bears on it. (5) The remaining 30,768 characters of Lambard's text, although the abstract already disclaims a proof.
